title: The Nizamiyya colleges
hookLine: the vizier Nizam al-Mulk founds colleges across the east, where al-Ghazali taught

cards: Nothing comes out. A well-known professor stands up to lecture in Baghdad, and he cannot speak. His tongue simply won't move.
He tries again on other days; the words won't come. He can barely eat. The doctors say the trouble started in his heart, and no medicine of theirs will reach it.
That professor was Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, and he tells this story himself, in a short book about his search for certainty. His prized teaching chair was at a college in Baghdad called the Nizamiyya.
Today's word is the kind of school it was: madrasah.

teach.b: Madrasah is simply the Arabic for a place of study, a school. In everyday Arabic it can still mean the school a child walks to in the morning.

teach.h: ENDOWED: A ROOM, A TEACHER, FOOD.
teach.b: But in Islamic history it also names something particular: a college, with a building, teachers paid to teach, students given a room and food, the whole thing supported by a waqf, an endowment set aside for good.
Nizam al-Mulk was a Persian vizier, the chief minister of the Seljuk sultans. He set up colleges in Baghdad and in other cities of the eastern lands, and they carried his name: the Nizamiyya.
A student who could recite and understand could find a place to live and a teacher, paid for by the endowment rather than by his own family.
That's where today's line comes from, a college in every city: a picture, not a count.

Al-Ghazali was one of its great teachers. Then, by his own account, he walked away. He left the chair, the students and the reputation, and set out to travel and to practice what he had been teaching.
Later he did teach again. In his telling, books had taught him what the Sufis said about the path, but walking it was something no book could do for him.
So he left the college for the road. And some of the books he wrote after leaving are still studied in madrasahs.

how: Madrasahs today range from children's Qur'an classes to colleges of Islamic law and theology, and some are supported by endowments (waqf) and gifts from their communities.

practice: Bring to mind a school, a teacher, a library or a mosque class that helped you learn, and ask who paid for the building, who swept the floor, who gave so you could sit there. Let one of them come clearly to mind.
If you pray, ask good for them; if you don't, thank them in your head.

wordCard.voice: Madrasah. A place of study, a school. In history, a college with teachers, students and an endowment to keep it going, like Nizam al-Mulk's. Today's word.
